issues.legal_issue: A person interested who did not file objections under Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, cannot challenge the acquisition on the ground that the objections were not properly heard or considered, absent a defect affecting the acquisition as a whole.
A purchaser who acquires land after publication of a notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, lacks standing to challenge the acquisition.

A landowner who voluntarily accepts compensation without reserving the right to pursue pending Section 5A objections is barred by acquiescence from continuing to challenge the acquisition on procedural grounds.
Official records showing service of hearing notices attract the presumption that official acts were regularly performed, and the objector bears the burden of proving ineffective service.
Failure to serve a hearing notice does not by itself invalidate an acquisition unless the landowner demonstrates resulting prejudice.
The Collector may consolidate and decide similar Section 5A objections together, provided the consolidation does not impair fair consideration of the objections.
The omission of a formal rejection order for some objections does not invalidate an acquisition where the objections were otherwise considered and the omission caused no material prejudice.
Land falling within an abadi area is not legally immune from acquisition, and its exemption is a matter of government policy and discretion.

Procedural deficiencies in a Section 5A inquiry do not warrant annulment of an acquisition where there has been substantial compliance and reversal would undermine the public interest after substantial completion and investment.

Where the land acquisition process remained pending when the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 came into force, compensation is payable under Section 24(1) and the relevant provisions of that Act.
